project-zaman/characters/protagonists/su.content:
Subject-002
Tags: project-zaman characters character wanderer subject-002 body trauma active
“The Vessel”

The body remained. It walks. It persists. It cannot understand what is missing, because what is missing is the part that would have understood.

MBTI Profile: ISTJ  (Not judged completely)
Designation: Subject-002 (Axios classification)
Origin: Created from the original MC during the Oscillation of Eras
Role: Neutral wanderer; holds no known allegiance
Status: Active; observed only at a distance

Overview
Subject-002 is the body-dominant fragment created when the original MC fractured during the Oscillation of Eras.
He inherited the original body, the straitjacket, its conditioned responses, and the accumulated physical consequences of captivity. What he did not inherit was the same emotional, moral, and spiritual continuity carried by Subject-001.
Subject-002 is therefore not simply the original MC without his memories.
He is the physical continuation of a person whose inner meaning has been removed from him.
His movements, habits, and reactions are shaped by experiences he cannot consciously interpret. The body remembers confinement, pain, procedure, and survival, but it cannot explain why those memories exist.
He does not serve the cult.
He does not oppose it.
He wanders through the post-Oscillation world without visible destination or allegiance, continuing because continuation is the deepest instruction remaining within him.

The Vessel
Subject-002 is frequently described as a soulless vessel, though the term is not entirely precise.
He possesses awareness, instinct, and behavioral continuity. He can observe, react, avoid danger, and move according to recognizable patterns. What he lacks is the cohesive inner structure that once transformed those actions into identity, meaning, attachment, and moral choice.
He carries:


The original MC’s body


Procedural and muscular memory


Conditioned fear responses


Physical trauma


Defensive instinct


Fragments of the shadow form


Familiar habits without remembered purpose


The instinct to survive without understanding why survival matters


Subject-002 is not lifeless.
He is life reduced to continuation.
Where Subject-001 asks what his existence means, Subject-002 does not appear capable of forming the question.

The Straitjacket
The straitjacket belonged to the original MC.
He wore it for so long that it became a second skin: a physical record of restraint and of the institution’s attempt to contain someone it could classify but never understand.
When the fission occurred, the straitjacket remained with the body.
On the original MC, it restrained a living interior.
On Subject-002, it becomes a memorial.
The fabric preserves the shape of suffering even when the person who understood that suffering is no longer fully present within it. Its buckles, folds, stains, and pressure points carry a history Subject-002 cannot narrate.
He does not wear it as a symbol.
He may not even understand that it can be removed.
The garment persists because it has become embedded in his bodily identity. It is no longer merely something placed upon him. It is part of the condition through which the body understands itself.
Subject-002 carries the evidence of captivity without access to the consciousness that once named it as captivity.
He is the bruise without the nerve.

Nature
Subject-002 displays an ISTJ fission profile: methodical, repetitive, structured, and oriented toward consistency.
These qualities should not be understood as a complete personality in the ordinary sense. They are the organized residue of a person whose emotional and moral continuity has been displaced.
He operates through:


Pattern


Routine


Physical memory


Environmental observation


Repetition


Threat recognition


The logic of immediate survival


His actions may appear deliberate, but their purpose remains unclear.
He may repeat routes without knowing where they lead. He may avoid rooms associated with experimentation without remembering what occurred inside them. He may react violently to restraint while showing no visible anger.
His behavior is not random.
It follows rules whose origin has been forgotten.
Subject-002 is therefore neither fully directionless nor consciously purposeful. He is guided by structures embedded too deeply in the body to require thought.

Bodily Memory
Subject-002 remembers through sensation rather than narrative.
He does not appear to possess a coherent account of the original MC’s captivity. Instead, the past survives within him as physical response.
A sound may cause his posture to change.
A clinical instrument may provoke immediate withdrawal.
A familiar corridor may redirect his movement before he consciously observes it.
A hand reaching toward the straitjacket may trigger defensive aggression.
These responses suggest that the body has preserved experiences the mind cannot access as ordinary memory.
Subject-002 may not remember being restrained.
His body remembers how restraint begins.
He may not remember pain as an event.
His body remembers how to prepare for it.
This distinction is essential to his role. Subject-002 does not carry the interpretation of trauma.
He carries its reflexes.

Neutrality
Subject-002 holds no known allegiance.
He does not serve Anthropos, Axios, or Gibborim, even though his behavior was shaped by their procedures. Neither does he consciously resist them.
This neutrality is not balance, wisdom, or moral distance.
It is the absence of an internal framework through which allegiance could acquire meaning.
To serve would require belief.
To rebel would require judgment.
Subject-002 appears to possess neither in a complete form.
He may attack cult personnel if they attempt to restrain him. He may ignore them if they do not interfere with his movement. He may pass through the ruins of their facilities without curiosity, revenge, or recognition.
His behavior is governed by proximity, disturbance, and bodily threat rather than ideology.
He is not loyal.
He is not forgiving.
He simply does not organize the world through either concept.

Wandering
Subject-002 moves continually through the fractured world.
His routes appear systematic, though their purpose is unknown. He may be following residual patterns from the original MC’s captivity, responding to disturbances caused by the Oscillation, or moving toward something his body recognizes but his mind cannot identify.
Possible interpretations of his wandering include:


Repeating an abandoned procedural route


Searching for a location associated with bodily safety


Following traces of Subject-001


Responding to the remains of Silent Connection


Returning unconsciously toward the facility


Re-enacting the original MC’s desire to escape


Moving without destination because stopping was never permitted


The narrative does not initially confirm which interpretation is correct.
What matters is that Subject-002 never appears hurried.
He moves with the consistency of a process that does not expect to end.

Sightings
Subject-002 is not encountered directly during the early narrative.
He is seen at a distance.
The straitjacket makes him identifiable. Distance keeps him unreadable.
He may appear:


At the edge of a ruined settlement


Standing beyond a threshold


Crossing an exposed landscape


Watching from within an inaccessible structure


Moving along a distant ridge


Disappearing behind architecture before Subject-001 can approach


He does not call out.
He does not signal.
He does not appear to invite pursuit, though he may sometimes remain visible long enough to ensure he has been noticed.
The uncertainty surrounding these sightings prevents both Subject-001 and the player from immediately determining whether he is an observer, threat, guide, or hallucination.
Every appearance should feel intentional.
None should explain itself.

Recognition
For Subject-001, sightings of Subject-002 are among the most disorienting events in the narrative.
Something about the figure produces recognition without memory.
The posture is familiar.
The proportions are familiar.
The straitjacket evokes fear before Subject-001 understands what it represents.
Subject-001 may experience:


Physical discomfort that does not originate from his current body


Memories from an impossible point of view


Recognition of movements he has never consciously performed


The sensation of seeing himself from outside


Grief without an identifiable object


Fear that Subject-002 is what he will eventually become


Subject-001 initially interprets this familiarity as supernatural connection, temporal distortion, or evidence that Subject-002 has been following him.
He does not yet understand that he is looking at the body through which his inherited soul once experienced the world.

Relationship to Subject-001
Subject-001 and Subject-002 are not twins, copies, or independent experiments.
They are incompatible continuations of the same destroyed person.





































Subject-001Subject-002Carries the soulCarries the original bodyPreserves emotional meaningPreserves physical consequenceInherits empathy and moral continuityInherits conditioning and defensive instinctRemembers through feelingRemembers through sensationPossesses the DesertPossesses bodily continuityCarries Alyna’s final chargeCarries the body that heard itSearches for identityContinues without defining one
Subject-001 is the fragment most capable of understanding what the original MC endured.
Subject-002 is the fragment that physically endured it.
Neither possesses the whole truth.
Subject-001 may initially regard Subject-002 as an empty vessel and therefore as something less than himself. The eventual discovery of Subject-002’s bodily memory complicates that judgment.
The body is not merely an abandoned container.
It also remembers.

The Shadow Form
Subject-002 inherits significant traces of the original MC’s shadow form.
Before the Oscillation, the shadow form developed as a defensive response to repeated suffering. It allowed the original MC to act without fear, empathy, or hesitation when his compassionate self could no longer endure what was happening.
After the fracture, aspects of this state remain embedded within Subject-002’s survival mechanisms.
This may manifest as:


Sudden and efficient violence


Extreme resistance to restraint


Indifference to injury


Rapid threat assessment


Minimal hesitation once provoked


Continued movement despite physical damage


Lack of visible emotional escalation before attacking


Subject-002 is not constantly aggressive.
His violence is reactive, economical, and impersonal.
He does not attack out of hatred.
He removes obstacles.
This makes him dangerous in a manner fundamentally different from an antagonist. He does not pursue cruelty, power, or revenge.
He simply lacks the moral hesitation that would make violence difficult.

Alyna
Subject-002 carries the body that knew Alyna, but not the soul that fully understood what she meant.
Her voice, touch, presence, and routines may remain within him as physical familiarity. He may respond to objects associated with her, pause in places she once occupied, or recognize the rhythm of her lullaby without recalling its source.
These reactions do not necessarily constitute conscious grief.
They are remnants of recognition preserved below interpretation.
Subject-001 inherits the bond.
Subject-002 inherits its physical history.
One remembers why she mattered.
The other may remember how it felt when she entered the room.
This division makes Alyna one of the strongest possible points of resonance between the two subjects.
She is the person through whom soul and body may still recognize the same absence differently.

Narrative Function
Subject-002 serves as a living contradiction to Subject-001’s claim of continuity.
Subject-001 possesses the soul, empathy, and emotional memory of the original MC. He is therefore inclined to view himself as the rightful continuation of that life.
Subject-002 challenges this assumption merely by existing.
The original MC was not only his feelings, values, and relationships.
He was also a body.
That body was restrained, injured, conditioned, and forced to endure. It cannot be dismissed as an empty shell simply because it lacks the same inner voice.
Subject-002 therefore raises several questions:


Does personhood belong more strongly to the soul or the body?


Can trauma remain meaningful when it is no longer consciously understood?


Does physical continuity create a legitimate claim to identity?


Is Subject-002 empty, or does he represent a form of personhood Subject-001 cannot recognize?


What would reunion mean when neither fragment can safely contain the other?


Subject-002 does not answer these questions.
He embodies them.

Significance
Subject-002’s existence asks:

Where does trauma go when the soul leaves?

It remains in the body.
It remains in posture, instinct, avoidance, repetition, and the expectation of pain. It remains in the straitjacket and in the movements learned beneath it.
Subject-002 does not suffer in the same reflective sense as Subject-001. He does not grieve his condition or articulate what was taken from him.
Yet this does not mean the damage has vanished.
He is the form trauma takes when meaning has been separated from sensation.
He carries suffering without possessing the language through which suffering becomes a story.
His existence is not peaceful.
It is unresolved.

Core Mystery
Subject-002’s central mystery is not whether he is alive.
It is whether anything within him can still become a self.
His behavior suggests more than machinery but less than complete personhood. The longer he persists, the more difficult it becomes to determine whether he is merely repeating inherited patterns or slowly developing choices of his own.
The distinction may initially be invisible.
A repeated route may eventually change.
A defensive reaction may become restraint.
A distant sighting may become deliberate contact.
The smallest deviation would carry enormous significance.
It would suggest that the vessel is no longer merely continuing.
It is becoming.


The soul left. The body continued. Somewhere along the road, continuation may have begun to resemble a will of its own.

The Founder of the Oasis
Tags: project-zaman characters character founder father-figure oasis survivors survival deceased


                  
                  Current Boundary 
                  
                

This page records the founder’s confirmed role without overdefining his name, politics, or personal history.



Overview
The Founder of the Oasis was the first father figure of The Oasis and one of the main reasons the early faction remained united.
He had strong Arab descent, giving the faction’s origin a human and cultural root rather than leaving it as a purely symbolic organization.
His importance does not depend on being flawless. He matters because the survivors understood him as a stabilizing presence: someone who made the original oath feel personal, practical, and worth preserving.

Legacy
After his death, The Oasis lost more than a leader.
It lost the person who had embodied the faction’s shared promise. Without him, the same oath split into two competing interpretations:

The Order of the Oasis claimed discipline, protection, and direct continuity with his original duty.
The Mirage rejected the belief that protection alone could fulfill his purpose after the world had already changed.

Both child factions speak from grief. Both claim part of his legacy. Neither fully replaces what he held together.

Writing Boundary
Keep his page restrained until the story gives him more direct scenes.
For now, his strongest use is as the emotional origin of The Oasis: the father figure whose absence made the schism possible.

project-zaman/characters/supporting/the-.title: The Hope Entity
project-zaman/characters/supporting/the-.content:
The Hope Entity
Tags: project-zaman characters character supporting hope-entity hope identity dormant
“The Child Before the Number”

It was not lost. It was left behind. There is a difference, and that difference determines whether retrieval remains possible.

Nature: Psychological entity; the preserved childhood self of the original MC
Location: The Desert, Subject-001’s inner psychological landscape
Inherited by: Subject-001
Status: Dormant; awaiting reconnection

Overview
The Hope Entity is the preserved childhood self of the original MC as he existed before extraction, classification, and prolonged experimentation.
Before the number.
Before the straitjacket.
Before the Oscillation divided him into incomplete fragments.
It remains within the Desert, the psychological landscape inherited by Subject-001. Unlike a conventional memory, it has not been distorted by the original MC’s later suffering. It preserves the structure of the person he was before the cult imposed a new identity upon him.
It is called the Hope Entity not because it is cheerful or optimistic, but because it represents the condition required for hope to exist at all:

A self that can survive change without being reduced to what was done to it.

It is the only known aspect of the original MC that remained whole after the fission.

Nature
The Hope Entity is neither a ghost nor a hallucination. It is not a memory that can simply be recalled, nor an independent consciousness living inside Subject-001.
It is a psychic remainder: a preserved configuration of identity that the extraction process failed to reach.
The cult stripped away the original MC’s name, freedom, safety, and sense of context. However, the Hope Entity formed before those things could be fully understood as possessions and therefore before they could be consciously experienced as losses.
What remained was not innocence in its sentimental sense.
It was the earliest internal structure through which the original MC understood himself.
The Hope Entity does not age. It does not wander through the Desert in search of Subject-001, nor does it actively call to him. It remains present in the way a buried root remains present: hidden, structurally intact, and capable of reconnecting with whatever survives above it.

The Desert
The Desert is Subject-001’s internal psychological landscape, inherited from the original MC following the fission.
Its terrain is not geographically stable. Distance, weather, light, and scale shift according to Subject-001’s psychological condition. The Desert does not merely reflect emotion; it expresses the degree of coherence between his fragmented identities.
The Hope Entity exists somewhere within this landscape, but its apparent distance is never fixed.
It draws nearer when:


Subject-001’s empathy remains dominant.


His original form is stable.


He accepts painful memories without surrendering control to them.


His thoughts enter the state of calm required by his miracles.


It becomes more distant when:


His identity begins to fracture.


His form becomes unstable.


Grief, fear, or rage overwhelms his sense of self.


He rejects parts of his history in order to preserve a simpler identity.


The Hope Entity does not physically move.
Subject-001’s ability to perceive and approach it changes.
Reaching it requires the same internal stillness once demanded by the original MC’s miracles. Force, urgency, and obsession only distort the path further.

Reconnection
Reconnection with the Hope Entity does not restore the original MC.
The Irreversibility Principle makes such restoration impossible. The child who once existed cannot return unchanged, and the events that followed cannot be erased from him.
Reconnection instead produces integration.
Subject-001 takes the preserved foundation of his childhood identity into his present, fragmented self. The Hope Entity becomes part of a consciousness that also contains grief, guilt, knowledge, violence, and the consequences of the Oscillation.
The result is not a perfectly healed person.
It is a person capable of holding his complete history without allowing one part of that history to consume everything else.
He can carry:


The fracture that created him.


Alyna’s death.


The truth of Subject-002.


The cult’s manipulation.


The person he was before any of them.


The Hope Entity does not erase Subject-001’s wounds.
It prevents those wounds from becoming his only identity.

Meaning of Hope
Within Project ZAMAN, hope is not the belief that suffering will be reversed or that events will eventually resolve themselves favorably.
Hope is the capacity to continue without amputating the unbearable parts of the self.
It is not certainty that the future will improve.
It is the ability to enter that future as something more than the sum of one’s injuries.
The Hope Entity embodies this principle. It offers no escape from the past, no restoration of innocence, and no return to an untouched state.
It offers continuity.

Role Within the Fission
The existence of the Hope Entity answers one of the darkest questions raised by Soul Fission:

Was any part of the original MC inherited by neither fragment?

Yes.
The original childhood self was not divided cleanly between Subject-001 and Subject-002. It remained preserved within the Desert, outside the immediate division of body, soul, and trauma.





















FragmentPrimary InheritanceSubject-001The soul, empathy, moral continuity, and griefSubject-002The body, conditioned responses, the straitjacket, and accumulated traumaThe Hope EntityThe foundational self that existed before extraction and classification
Subject-001 carries what the original MC believed and felt.
Subject-002 carries what was physically and psychologically done to him.
The Hope Entity carries the person who existed before either inheritance became necessary.

Narrative Significance
The Hope Entity is not a hidden cure waiting to undo the Oscillation. Treating it as one would contradict the narrative’s central metaphysical rule.
Its purpose is not restoration, but completion.
Until Subject-001 reconnects with it, his identity remains organized around fragments inherited from catastrophe. He may feel empathy, experience grief, and recognize the truth of his origin, yet still lack the internal foundation required to understand those experiences as parts of a single life.
The Hope Entity provides that foundation.
It does not tell Subject-001 who he should become.
It allows him to recognize that he existed before others began defining him.


It is not waiting to be rescued. It is waiting to be remembered.

project-zaman/creative/ideas/ideas-inbox.content:
Ideas Inbox
Tags: project-zaman creative creative ideas open


                  
                  Purpose of this folder 
                  
                

Unfiltered capture. Nothing here is canon, and nothing here needs to be finished or defended. When an idea is accepted it moves to Lore/, World/, or Production/ and gets removed from this list.
Keeping this folder separate is what lets the rest of the vault stay confirmed.



How to Use This
Three states, marked inline so nothing gets mistaken for settled lore:

#idea — raw, unexamined
#considering — being weighed, may conflict with existing notes
#rejected — kept on purpose, with the reason, so it does not get re-proposed in six months

Rejected ideas are worth more than they look. Half the value of a long project is remembering why you said no.

Open Threads Worth Thinking About
These come from questions the vault has already raised, not from anywhere new. They are prompts, not proposals.
On the ending — Open Gaps #08 is the largest gap in the project. Worth capturing several incompatible endings here before committing to one, since the Irreversibility Principle rules out most conventional resolutions by design.
On Subject-002 — currently only ever seen at a distance. What would it cost, narratively, for that to change once? Whatever the answer, it should be expensive.
On Noam — Open Gaps #08 asks whether he is defeated, redeemed, or simply left behind. Themes argues the redemption question may no longer be meaningful, which is a harder and more interesting position than either defeat or redemption.
On the Hope Entity — it is explicitly not a cure. The Hope Entity warns that treating it as one contradicts the central metaphysical rule. Any idea that makes reconnection fix something should be checked against that.
On the factions — the Rebuild the Oasis path in The Oasis requires the player to prove both sides hold incomplete halves of the same answer. That structure could apply elsewhere in the game.
On the third miracle — silent connection across distance is the only ability that reaches other people. It is used twice and then never again in the current outline. It is the most underused idea in the vault.

Idea Capture Format
### <one-line idea>  #idea
 
**Touches:** [[ ]]
**Conflicts with:** <existing canon this would break, if any>
 
<a few sentences>
 
**Why it might work:**
**Why it might not:**

Rejected
Keep entries here permanently, with the reason.















IdeaWhy it was rejectedWhen(example) Restoring the pre-Oscillation world as an endingBreaks the Irreversibility Principle, which the whole project is built on—



                  
                  Do not let this folder leak 
                  
                

Everything in Lore/ and World/ should be treated as confirmed. Everything here should not. If an idea is promoted, delete it from this note when you move it, so it never exists in two states at once.

project-zaman/creative/influences/index.content:
Influences
Tags: project-zaman creative creative influences working


                  
                  Purpose of this folder 
                  
                

What Project ZAMAN is drawing from, and — more usefully — what it is not taking. An influence note that only lists what you liked will quietly turn the project into an imitation. Recording the boundary is the point.



Declared Influences
Lies of P
Named in Project Zaman as an aesthetic reference, and again in The Oasis: the survivor faction structure was partly inspired by the Sweepers and Bastards, collectively associated with the Stalkers.
Taken: the period-industrial aesthetic; the idea of scattered factions of survivors with opposed philosophies whom the player can side with, betray, or reconcile.
Not taken: the puppet/humanity framework. Project ZAMAN’s equivalent question is about a soul divided by contradiction, not a construct earning humanity.
Bloodborne
Named in Project Zaman as an aesthetic reference.
Taken: the aesthetic register — early-modern setting with a metaphysical horror beneath it, and institutions that were respectable before they were monstrous.
Not taken, and worth stating clearly: the cosmic-indifference stance. Project ZAMAN’s catastrophe is not caused by an inhuman outside force. It is caused by one man’s refusal to lose, on top of a century of institutional ambition. The horror here is entirely human, and Themes is explicit that the ending is adaptation rather than transcendence.

The Genre Tension Already Identified
Themes states the position directly: where many Soulslikes hand the player a broken world and ask them to restore an earlier order — lighting the fire, ending the cycle, reclaiming the throne — Project ZAMAN refuses that structure. There is no earlier order worth restoring.
That is a deliberate break from the genre it belongs to, and it is the most important influence note in the project: it defines the shape by what it declines to do.

Worth Documenting

Non-game influences. Nothing is recorded yet. The project’s real subject matter — institutional exploitation dressed as charity, identity erased by classification, grief that cannot be resolved — has more precedent in literature and history than in games.
The Masonic framing. Real fraternal-order structure is doing a lot of quiet work in the cult’s Anthropos/Gibborim/Axios split. Worth noting what was borrowed and what was invented.
The naming framework’s sources. Hebrew and Greek are used with specific intent in Gibborim and Anthropos. The Arabic register is declared and still empty.


Note Format
### <title> — <medium, year>
 
**Relevance:** Aesthetic / Structural / Thematic / Systems
 
## What It Does Well
 
## What Project ZAMAN Takes
 
## What Project ZAMAN Deliberately Does Not Take
<the section that keeps this project distinct>
 
## Where It Applies
[[ ]]



                  
                  The test to apply 
                  
                

For every influence, be able to finish the sentence: “This is like X, except —”. If the exception is hard to name, the influence is being copied rather than used.

Reference Library
Tags: project-zaman creative creative references working


                  
                  Purpose of this folder 
                  
                

Source material to consult while writing and building: research, terminology, visual reference, and technical documentation.
Distinct from Creative/Influences, which records works this project is responding to. This folder is for things you look up.



Research Needed
Areas the vault already depends on but has not yet grounded:
Period research — early 20th century
Institutional life, orphanages and their real record-keeping, domestic service and what a uniform meant socially, newspapers and how a story was placed or suppressed, harbor and dock work, underground and anonymous publishing. Alyna’s entire campaign in Story Structure rests on how small presses actually operated and how they were traced.
Language
Hebrew terms and transliteration for the Gibborim register. Greek for Anthropos and Axios. Arabic for the declared-but-empty register described in Symbols/Typography. Worth recording the source and transliteration for every term adopted, so nothing gets silently mangled later.
Fraternal orders
Real structure, degrees, and secrecy practices, to keep the three-layer cult believable and to be clear about where the fiction departs from the reality.
Clinical and archival writing
Axios’ voice depends on it. Real case notes, subject numbering conventions, and laboratory record formats would make its neutrality genuinely unsettling rather than stylized.
Technical
Engine documentation once the engine is chosen; the New Input System referenced in Project Zaman.

project-zaman/factions/anthropos.title: Anthropos
project-zaman/factions/anthropos.content:
Anthropos
Tags: project-zaman factions faction parent-faction authority anthropos head-family cult institutional-horror established

“In Service of All Mankind”

The cult’s public face: a humanitarian mask concealing a system of exploitation.

Origin: Greek, ánthrōpos, meaning “human being”
Layer: Parent institution; public-facing cult structure
Public Symbol: None
Children: Axios, Gibborim
Known family authority: Head Family

Overview
Anthropos presents itself as a philanthropic and intellectual order devoted to the advancement of humanity. It operates openly through legitimate institutions, including orphanages, academic sponsorships, medical initiatives, and civic development programs.
Behind this respectable exterior, Anthropos serves as the recruitment, observation, and acquisition arm of the cult’s inner order. It identifies individuals with unusual cognitive, spiritual, or metaphysical potential, then quietly places them within systems controlled by Gibborim.
Most members of Anthropos are unaware that Gibborim even exists.

Hierarchy
Anthropos is the parent structure used to organize the cult’s public and hidden branches.




















BranchRoleVisibilityAxiosScientific division; observes, classifies, and records soul-based phenomenaPublic-facing under Anthropos, but with restricted findingsGibborimPrivate esoteric order; assigns doctrine, ownership, and ultimate purposeHidden from most Anthropos members
In-world, this hierarchy is deceptive. Anthropos appears to be the parent authority, but Gibborim secretly directs the system from within. Axios functions as the technical child branch that gives Anthropos credibility while serving Gibborim’s deeper agenda.

Known Authority and Members
Anthropos should not receive a large member roster until the story clearly needs one. Its current authority structure works best when kept focused:





















Figure or groupRoleHead FamilyThe dynastic family line attached to Anthropos authority; currently centered on Noam and Noam’s Father.The Oath-KeeperThe active overseer who keeps Axios procedure and Gibborim doctrine aligned.NoamThe active heir and mirror antagonist shaped by the cult’s ideals.
This keeps the hierarchy readable: the Head Family represents inheritance and political pressure, while the oath-keeper represents command, discipline, and operational control.

Primary Functions


Operates institutions such as Ashbourne Children’s Home, presenting them as welfare programs while using them to identify and cultivate valuable candidates.


Monitors individuals who display rare cognitive abilities, spiritual sensitivity, or unusual soul-based characteristics.


Transfers selected subjects into controlled environments through adoption, sponsorship, employment, medical care, or academic placement.


Maintains public legitimacy through charity, civic service, and intellectual patronage.


Redirects suspicion toward administrative failures, isolated misconduct, or unfortunate circumstances.


Acts as a protective outer layer, ensuring that public scrutiny never reaches Gibborim.



Institutional Character
Anthropos is polished, disciplined, and idealistic in its presentation. Its rhetoric revolves around human potential, collective progress, moral responsibility, and enlightened stewardship.
To the public, it resembles a progressive philanthropic order composed of scholars, patrons, physicians, educators, and civic leaders. Its members speak sincerely of improving society and guiding humanity toward a more prosperous future.
That sincerity is what makes Anthropos dangerous.
Most of its operatives are not sadists, conspirators, or willing servants of evil. They genuinely believe their work benefits humanity. They see vulnerable children as lives to be guided, gifted individuals as talents to be cultivated, and sacrifice as an unfortunate necessity of progress.
They do not know what waits beyond the threshold.


The smile that conceals the threshold.

project-zaman/factions/anthropos/axios.title: Axios
project-zaman/factions/anthropos/axios.content:
Axios
Tags: project-zaman factions faction child-faction overseen axios cult science established
“The Science Division”

The cult’s analytical engine. It does not ask whether something should be done, only how precisely it can be observed, measured, and repeated.

Origin: Greek, áxios, meaning “worthy”
Parent: Anthropos
Layer: Public-facing scientific division
Private Counterpart: None
Operational Overseer: The Oath-Keeper
Symbol: A black serpent, depicted without hook, fang, or ornament

Overview
Axios is the scientific and empirical division of the cult, operating publicly beneath the Anthropos banner as a legitimate research institution.
Its name frames measurement as worth: what can be observed, repeated, and archived becomes worthy of attention. What cannot be measured is either ignored or forced into a form Axios can record.
Unlike the other branches, Axios possesses no concealed identity. Its purpose remains unchanged across both the public and inner layers. It observes, classifies, documents, and systematizes every phenomenon the cult encounters, including individuals with rare cognitive or soul-based abilities.
Axios provides the intellectual credibility displayed by Anthropos and the technical foundation required by Gibborim. Under the oath-keeper’s oversight, Axios determines what subjects are, how they function, and how they may be reproduced or controlled.

Primary Functions


Conducts research into soul-based phenomena, including Immaculate Thought and its effects on the human mind, body, and soul.


Develops and maintains the cult’s subject classification, identification, and numbering systems.


Records Soul Fission, the Oscillation of Eras, and all observable consequences caused by the misuse of Immaculate Thought.


Designs, operates, and maintains experimental chambers, containment systems, preservation equipment, and monitoring instruments.


Oversees the technical handling of subjects before, during, and after experimentation.


Produces clinical reports and findings for Gibborim while withholding sensitive material from the broader Anthropos institution.


Archives failed procedures, abnormal outcomes, and contradictions without moral interpretation.



Institutional Character
Axios is the most quietly dangerous of the cult’s divisions because it possesses no true ideology of its own.
Its members are scientists, physicians, archivists, mathematicians, and engineers who have separated empirical procedure from moral consequence. They do not consider themselves executioners or zealots. They consider themselves observers.
The horror of Axios lies in its neutrality.
Axios would document the collapse of a human soul with the same composure used to record a pulse, temperature, or mechanical fault. It neither celebrates suffering nor condemns it. Every scream becomes data. Every death becomes a recorded outcome. Every failure becomes the foundation of a more precise experiment.
It does not desire catastrophe.
It simply refuses to stop measuring it.
Where Anthropos smiles and Gibborim commands, Axios records.

Naming and Language
Axios has no Hebrew inner name because it belongs entirely to the cult’s public and scientific register. Its terminology remains clinical, procedural, and deliberately stripped of spiritual implication.
Its reports avoid ritual language, even when documenting metaphysical events. Souls become measurable structures. Gifts become cognitive anomalies. Human beings become subjects, specimens, and numbered cases.
The subject identification system, including designations such as Subject-001 and Subject-002, originated within Axios’ archives before being adopted and reinterpreted by Gibborim within its esoteric hierarchy.

Symbol
Axios is represented by a black serpent.
Unlike traditional serpent imagery, it bears no hook, crown, open mouth, or visible fang. It is shown as silent and controlled, suggesting observation, precision, continuity, and knowledge without declared intent.
The serpent does not strike.
It watches.


It did not build the threshold. It measured its exact dimensions.

project-zaman/factions/anthropos/gibbori.title: Gibborim
project-zaman/factions/anthropos/gibbori.content:
Gibborim
Tags: project-zaman factions faction child-faction overseen gibborim cult doctrine established

“We Who Stood Beyond the Threshold”

The cult’s inner order. Those who discovered what Immaculate Thought truly was and chose to weaponize it regardless.

Origin: Hebrew, gibbōrīm, meaning “mighty ones”
Parent: Anthropos
Layer: Private esoteric order
Operational Overseer: The Oath-Keeper
Symbol: A white serpent with a hissing mouth and an anchor-hook tail

Overview
Gibborim is the concealed authority at the heart of the cult.
Where Anthropos speaks publicly of elevating humanity, Gibborim seeks dominion over the deepest capacities of the human soul. Its members do not merely study soul-based phenomena. They determine how such phenomena should be interpreted, controlled, and exploited.
The Oath-Keeper acts as one of its key operational authorities, keeping Gibborim’s doctrine connected to the technical work performed by Axios.
Gibborim understands that Immaculate Thought is not a method of manipulating time. It is an extreme state of cognition in which thought approaches absolute speed, clarity, and internal consistency.
The order nevertheless preserves the language of temporal control.
This deception is deliberate. By controlling how Immaculate Thought is described, Gibborim controls how subjects understand their own abilities, their failures, and the consequences imposed upon them.
The false interpretation is not an error within the system.
It is part of the system.

Primary Functions


Directs Anthropos through intermediaries, private councils, and carefully separated chains of authority.


Selects individuals identified by Anthropos and classified by Axios for further observation, containment, or experimentation.


Oversees the extraction, conditioning, and exploitation of individuals with rare cognitive or soul-based abilities.


Assigns ritual meaning and hierarchical significance to Axios’ clinical subject classifications.


Controls access to research involving Immaculate Thought, Soul Fission, and the Oscillation of Eras.


Enforces the Irreversibility Principle as doctrine, acknowledging that the Oscillation cannot be undone and restructuring its plans around that permanence.


Determines which discoveries are revealed, concealed, reinterpreted, or erased.


Maintains authority over the experimental chamber system, including the Eleventh Chamber, where Alyna’s body remains preserved.



Institutional Character
Gibborim is not outwardly fanatical.
It is ceremonial, restrained, and coldly composed.
Its members speak as custodians of dangerous knowledge rather than worshippers of forbidden power. They believe that what they have uncovered is too consequential to be entrusted to ordinary institutions, public morality, or individual choice.
Within Gibborim, cruelty is rarely described as cruelty. It is framed as containment, stewardship, preservation, or necessity.
The deeper a member rises within the order, the easier it becomes to interpret suffering as evidence of responsibility. Every sacrifice confirms the importance of the work. Every catastrophe becomes proof that only Gibborim possesses the discipline required to continue it.
Its members do not believe they have abandoned morality.
They believe they have surpassed the need for ordinary morality.
Noam is among the order’s most complete creations: raised within its doctrine, shaped to inherit its authority, and taught to conceal fear beneath perfect composure. His conviction is genuine precisely because it was cultivated before he could distinguish belief from obedience.

Doctrine
At the center of Gibborim’s worldview is the belief that knowledge creates ownership.
To understand a phenomenon more deeply than another person is, in their doctrine, to earn the right to govern it. This principle extends beyond machines, institutions, and scientific discoveries. It applies equally to minds, bodies, memories, and souls.
A gifted individual is therefore not regarded as the owner of their ability.
They are regarded as its temporary vessel.
Gibborim considers itself the rightful custodian of whatever exists within that vessel.

Naming and Language
Gibborim uses Hebrew for its rituals, ranks, doctrines, chambers, and esoteric concepts. This linguistic boundary separates the order’s private operations from the Greek-derived language used by Anthropos in public.
Axios’ reports remain clinical, but Gibborim absorbs their classifications into a ceremonial framework. Designations such as Subject-001 and Subject-002 originate as neutral archival identifiers before being transformed into markers of hierarchy, purpose, and spiritual significance.
Within the inner order, a number is never merely a number.
It represents sequence, proximity, failure, inheritance, and perceived worth.
The protagonist’s incomplete integration into this system is treated as both an anomaly and a threat. He exists within Gibborim’s records, yet resists the meaning the order assigns to him.
By surviving outside that meaning, he exposes the possibility that their system is neither inevitable nor absolute.

Symbol
Gibborim is represented by a white serpent with an open, hissing mouth and a tail shaped into an anchor-like hook.
The white coloring suggests purity, revelation, and divine authority, while concealing the violence beneath those claims. Its open mouth represents doctrine spoken as command. The hooked tail represents possession: once something crosses into Gibborim’s reach, it is secured, restrained, and drawn inward.
Unlike Axios’ silent black serpent, Gibborim’s serpent announces its authority.
It does not merely observe knowledge.
It claims it.


They did not fall beyond the threshold. They stepped.

project-zaman/factions/the-oasis.title: The Oasis
project-zaman/factions/the-oasis.content:
The Oasis
Tags: project-zaman factions faction parent-faction oasis survivors survival founder-legacy fractured


                  
                  Meaning of the Name 
                  
                

The name The Oasis represents the faction’s original purpose.
An oasis is a rare place of safety in a hostile land: shelter, peace, and the essence of life, water. In the same way, The Oasis swore to become a refuge for what remained of humanity after the Catastrophe, also known as the Oscillation of Eras.



Overview
The Oasis was founded by survivors who wanted to protect what remained of humanity after the Catastrophe.
Its first father figure was The Founder of the Oasis, a leader of strong Arab descent whose presence made the original oath feel personal rather than abstract.
Its early work combined four duties:

Explore dangerous regions.
Recover useful resources and relics.
Record information about the changed world.
Protect the remaining traces of human civilization.

The faction did not collapse through a calm or mutual separation. After its founder died, two beliefs inside the group became impossible to reconcile:

One side sought knowledge as the path to salvation.
The other remained loyal to the original oath of protecting humanity.

The original Oasis was succeeded by two opposing child factions:




















Child factionCore beliefCentral weaknessThe Order of the OasisHumanity must first protect confirmed survivors, territory, and supplies.Denial: it avoids the uncertain fate of those lost through the Fabrication Demise.The MirageHumanity can only survive by uncovering the truth behind the Catastrophe.Chaos: it gathers evidence faster than it can understand or apply it.
Neither side believes it destroyed The Oasis. Each believes the other proved that The Oasis had already ceased to exist.


                  
                  Inspiration 
                  
                

The faction was partly inspired by the Sweepers and Bastards, collectively associated with the Stalkers in Lies of P.



Hierarchy
The Oasis is the parent faction. After the schism, it exists in three forms:






























LayerStatusFunction in the storyThe original OasisBroken legacyThe founding oath and shared history both child factions claim.The Founder of the OasisDeceased father figureThe personal authority whose absence allows the schism to form.The Order of the OasisActive child factionDiscipline, protection, territory, and resource security.The MirageActive child factionExploration, field records, forbidden sites, and the search for answers.
The parent note should hold shared history, faction-wide systems, and outcome logic. The child notes hold each faction’s ideology, behavior, locations, and weaknesses.

The Schism
The conflict began when two influential groups disagreed over which problem humanity had to solve first.
Conditions throughout the world were becoming worse. Many members had already been lost, including the founder of The Oasis, who had served as a fatherly figure to the survivors. With the founder gone, the faction slowly lost its unity.
Some members wanted to change the old oath. They believed The Oasis should actively search for knowledge, investigate the Catastrophe, and uncover a possible path toward humanity’s salvation.
Others rejected this. They argued that knowledge alone offered no immediate protection. In their view, the faction’s duty was to confront the dangers already threatening humanity rather than spend its remaining strength chasing answers that might never save anyone.
The First Departure
The loyalists came to see the original Oasis as impure. To them, the faction had not merely changed its methods; it had betrayed the founder’s purpose.
They separated and formed The Order of the Oasis.
The name was both a declaration and a judgment. By calling themselves an Order, they presented their faction as the disciplined continuation of the founder’s original duty.
The Naming of The Mirage
Those left behind viewed the Order’s departure as selfish, arrogant, and self-righteous. From their perspective, the loyalists had abandoned their companions during a crisis, claimed sole ownership over the founder’s legacy, and condemned anyone who believed the old methods had failed.
In time, they accepted a new name: The Mirage.
The name came from a bitter conclusion:

If The Oasis is no longer there, then what remains must be The Mirage.

To them, the safety promised by The Oasis had always been temporary. Its stability was an illusion, and the original oath could only delay humanity’s destruction rather than prevent it.

Shared Enemy
Despite their ideological conflict, both child factions recognize Anthropos as their common enemy.
However, neither faction understands Anthropos’s true nature.
Only the player knows that the beings they call Anthropos are actually tied to Gibborim, the hidden authority behind the cult.
This hidden truth becomes especially important when members of either faction discover the player’s identity.

NPC Encounters
The player may encounter faction members during hostile confrontations, passive scenes, exploration events, or faction-related quests.
Every major NPC should have a clear:

Personality.
History.
Motivation.
Relationship with their faction.
Opinion of the opposing side.
Reaction to the player’s identity.

Some members may have personal relationships with people from the opposing faction. Former friends, relatives, mentors, and companions may now stand on opposite sides of the schism.
Most of these NPCs are not inherently cruel or evil. Their beliefs were shaped by loss, territory, duty, and the stories their faction told them after the founder died.
The schism should remain personal as well as ideological. Order members may believe former companions abandoned humanity’s immediate needs. Mirage members may believe the Order abandoned them first and then rewrote the meaning of loyalty.
Their accusations are strengthened by each faction’s visible failure:

Order members can point to years of Mirage expeditions that produced fragments, stories, and relics, but no dependable salvation.
Mirage members can point to the Order’s refusal to investigate the unconfirmed fate of the population lost through the Fabrication Demise.

Neither side is entirely wrong. Neither side is doing enough.

Solo and Grouped NPCs
Solo faction members are generally more:

Rebellious.
Capable.
Unpredictable.
Sharp-witted.
Willing to question orders.

Members encountered in groups are generally more:

Passive.
Disciplined.
Dependent on faction authority.
Protective of one another.
Likely to follow established commands.

These are broad tendencies rather than absolute rules.

Reactions to the Player’s Identity
When NPCs discover the player’s true identity, their reactions vary according to their personality, beliefs, and past experiences.
Some may become terrified. Others may immediately draw their weapons and attack.
During these confrontations, the player may be able to:

Kill the NPC.
Knock them unconscious.
Continue fighting until they surrender.
Spare them.
Question them.
Take their possessions.

After an NPC has been defeated or forced to surrender, the player may collect ordinary loot.
However, trying to loot them again provokes a stronger reaction. The remaining item holds personal value, and the NPC becomes furious if the player tries to take it.
This final possession may be:

A personal letter.
A family relic.
A faction insignia.
A photograph.
A journal page.
A unique tool.
A symbolic weapon.
Another collectible tied to the NPC’s history.

Taking these possessions may affect the NPC, their allies, and the player’s reputation.

Story Impact
The player’s treatment of The Mirage and the Order of the Oasis can significantly influence faction relationships and parts of the main story.





































PathOutcomeRemain a bystanderNeither faction fully trusts the player. The division continues, and faction opportunities stay limited.Support The MirageThe Mirage gains morale, respect, access to cult sites, and more evidence. The Order loses trust. Much of the evidence may still need outside interpretation.Support the Order of the OasisConfirmed survivors receive stronger protection. The Order gives the player access to protected regions and resources. The fate of the Fabrication Demise victims remains neglected.Infiltrate the Order for The MirageThe Mirage gains control through betrayal. The Order suffers heavy casualties, and surviving Order NPCs may become permanently hostile.Infiltrate The Mirage for the OrderThe Order strengthens its authority. The Mirage suffers heavy casualties, and cult-related knowledge may be lost. The surviving Mirage NPCs may become permanently hostile.Wage war against both factionsBoth sides suffer heavy casualties. The player gains material rewards but loses lasting support, making the story darker.Rebuild The OasisThe player reconciles both sides, restores the parent faction, and creates the strongest positive outcome.

Rebuild The Oasis
The player becomes the unifying figure both factions lost when the founder died.
This route does not declare either child faction wholly correct. It exposes the weakness in both interpretations:

The Order must accept that protecting only confirmed survivors while denying the uncertain fate of countless others is not true devotion to humanity.
The Mirage must accept that bravery, travel, and written records cannot replace knowledge, method, and disciplined analysis.

The player must prove that the two sides possess incomplete parts of the same solution:

The Order provides discipline, logistics, secure territory, and the means to protect people during a long investigation.
The Mirage provides field experience, access to forbidden regions, combat skill, and written records of discoveries the Order refused to pursue.

Only then can the two sides reunite and restore the original faction:
The Oasis
Consequences

Zero faction casualties.
Maximum morale.
Maximum respect from both sides.
The Mirage and the Order reunite.
Former enemies begin working together.
The restored Oasis combines exploration, research, protection, and recovery.
The restored Oasis becomes a major positive force in the main story.

This is the most difficult faction outcome. It requires the player to understand individual members, resolve personal conflicts, challenge both factions’ historical narratives, and earn trust from both sides.

project-zaman/factions/the-oasis/the-mir.title: The Mirage
project-zaman/factions/the-oasis/the-mir.content:
The Mirage
Tags: project-zaman factions faction child-faction mirage survivors knowledge chaos active

“The Refuge That Vanished”

If The Oasis is gone, then perhaps it was always a mirage.

Parent: The Oasis
Role: Exploratory successor faction
Primary territory: Cult facilities, abandoned laboratories, ritual sites, and temporally distorted regions
Opposing child faction: The Order of the Oasis

Overview
The Mirage consists mainly of those who remained after The Order of the Oasis separated from the original faction.
They had already begun rejecting the old oath. To them, simply protecting what remained of humanity would only delay humanity’s eventual destruction.
The Order’s departure deepened their resentment. They believed the loyalists had abandoned them while claiming moral superiority and sole ownership over the founder’s legacy.
Rather than continue using a name they believed had become hollow, they eventually called themselves The Mirage.

Meaning of the Name
The name The Mirage began as a bitter judgment of The Oasis.
A mirage resembles safety from a distance, but offers nothing when finally reached. Mirage members believe The Oasis promised salvation while only preserving humanity long enough for it to die more slowly.
They do not necessarily consider their own faction false. Instead, they carry the name as an admission that the old refuge was never enough.
Their central belief can be expressed as:

If The Oasis is gone, then perhaps it was always a mirage.


Ideology
The Mirage believes knowledge is the only meaningful path toward salvation.
Its members abandoned the faction’s traditional territories and began travelling toward locations connected to the cult responsible for the Catastrophe.
Their primary objective is to discover:

The origin of the Catastrophe.
The purpose of the cult’s experiments.
The truth behind the Oscillation of Eras.
A possible method of overcoming its effects.

To the Order, this pursuit is reckless and wasteful.
To The Mirage, refusing to search for answers is only a slower form of surrender.

Central Weakness: Chaos
The Mirage has the courage to enter places others avoid, but not the knowledge or discipline required to understand everything it finds.
Most of its members are capable fighters, gifted writers, or both. They can survive hostile expeditions, recover fragments of evidence, and record what they witness with care.
However, these abilities do not automatically make them investigators.
The faction lacks a consistent research method, shared analytical discipline, and enough understanding of the cult’s machinery, rituals, metaphysics, and experiments. Its members often return with damaged records, unexplained objects, contradictory accounts, and discoveries they cannot interpret.
As a result, The Mirage often mistakes movement for progress.
Its exploration is not meaningless. Its fighters keep expeditions alive, while its writers preserve details that might otherwise vanish. The tragedy is that the faction continues collecting evidence without the framework needed to turn that evidence into something useful for humanity.
The Mirage may be searching in the correct places, but in its current state, it does not know how to recognize the answer even if it finds one.

Common Locations
Members of The Mirage are usually encountered near:

Cult facilities.
Abandoned laboratories.
Ritual sites.
Temporally distorted regions.
Areas under strong cult influence.


General Behavior
Mirage members are often:

Independent.
Rebellious.
Sharp-witted.
Suspicious of authority.
Resentful of the Order’s claim to ideological purity.
Willing to break old laws in pursuit of the truth.
Usually skilled in combat, writing, or both.
Poorly equipped to analyze many of their own discoveries.
Prone to confusing exploration with meaningful progress.

Many members operate alone, although smaller exploration groups may also be encountered.

Working Visual Identity
The Mirage should look like a faction that crossed the map too many times and kept writing anyway.

























ElementDirectionPaletteSun-faded blue, ash gray, weathered black, and pale cloth.InsigniaA broken or wavering water-drop mark, as if the original Oasis symbol has become a heat-shimmer reflection.SilhouetteAsymmetrical travel gear, notebooks or scroll cases, wrapped limbs, field tools, and improvised protection.Material languageDust-stained fabric, cracked leather, handwritten tags, salvaged cult fragments, and repaired weapons.
The design should show courage, disorder, and accumulated evidence. They should look capable in the field, but never fully uniform.

Relationship to the Order
The Mirage views The Order of the Oasis as fearful, self-righteous, and morally incomplete.
Its members believe the Order abandoned the unknown victims of the Fabrication Demise by deciding only confirmed survivors were worth protecting. They can point to the Order’s refusal to investigate the unconfirmed population as proof that the old oath has narrowed into denial.
Even so, the Mirage needs what the Order preserves: discipline, supplies, safe territory, and a structure capable of protecting people during a long investigation.
That dependence is the heart of the reunification path in The Oasis.

project-zaman/factions/the-oasis/the-ord.title: The Order of the Oasis
project-zaman/factions/the-oasis/the-ord.content:
The Order of the Oasis
Tags: project-zaman factions faction child-faction order-of-the-oasis survivors protection denial active

“The Oath Preserved”

They kept the promise. They also narrowed the meaning of who deserved to be protected.

Parent: The Oasis
Common shortening: OOTO
Role: Protective successor faction
Primary territory: Settlements, supply routes, defensive outposts, and resource-gathering areas
Opposing child faction: The Mirage

Overview
The Order of the Oasis consists of those who remained loyal to the original foundation and its oath.
They were the first group to formally separate from the collapsing Oasis. Believing the parent faction had become ideologically impure, they claimed the founder’s principles and carried them into a new organization.
The Order believes humanity cannot afford to waste its remaining strength searching for uncertain answers. Its duty is to protect settlements, secure resources, defend vulnerable territory, and preserve what little stability remains.
To the Order, abandoning the original purpose of The Oasis would betray everything the founder built.
That conviction also makes the faction rigid. Its members often treat their interpretation of the founder’s oath as the only legitimate one, and may view former companions as corruptors rather than people responding differently to the same catastrophe.

Meaning of the Name
The word Order represents discipline, preservation, and ideological purity.
The faction does not consider itself a replacement for The Oasis. Its members see themselves as the rightful continuation of the parent faction after the original organization lost its way.
To its enemies, the name represents self-appointed authority and an attempt to monopolize the founder’s legacy.

Central Weakness: Denial
Despite claiming to protect humanity, the Order increasingly defines humanity only through the survivors and territories it can still see.
A vast portion of the human population remains unaccounted for after the Fabrication Demise. Their deaths have never been confirmed, yet the Order behaves as though nothing meaningful can be done for them. It avoids the possibility that some may still exist in altered, displaced, trapped, or otherwise unreachable states.
This creates a moral contradiction. The Order presents itself as humanity’s rightful protector while refusing to seriously investigate the fate of countless people simply because their condition cannot be verified.
This failure does not make the Order irrational. The Mirage has spent years exploring dangerous regions without producing a reliable method of rescue, reversal, or recovery. From the Order’s perspective, sacrificing resources needed by confirmed survivors for an unproven possibility would be another form of abandonment.
The Order’s failure is therefore not that it protects those who remain. Its failure is that protection has slowly become an excuse to stop asking who else might still be saved.

Common Locations
Members of the Order are usually encountered near:

Settlement regions.
Supply routes.
Defensive outposts.
Resource-gathering areas.
Former Anthropos bases.



                  
                  Note
                  
                

The game does not contain ordinary civilian populations. Settlement regions function as protected territories, faction outposts, or remnants of organized human activity.



General Behavior
Order members are often:

Disciplined.
Loyal.
Determined.
Protective of their territory.
Distrustful of those who question the original oath.
Convinced that compromise will weaken humanity further.
Reluctant to investigate populations whose survival cannot be confirmed.
Prone to disguising denial as practical restraint.

They are more commonly found in organized groups and tend to behave more cautiously than isolated Mirage members.

Working Visual Identity
The Order should look like a faction that maintains what it inherited.

























ElementDirectionPaletteDeep green, worn brass, off-white cloth, and dark leather.InsigniaAn upright water-drop mark held inside a square frame, suggesting discipline around refuge.SilhouettePractical layered uniforms, visible repair work, standardized straps, and clean insignia placement.Material languageReused military fabric, polished buckles, patched coats, and carefully maintained tools.
The design should show care, order, and pressure. Nothing should feel ornamental for its own sake.

Relationship to The Mirage
The Order views The Mirage as reckless, disloyal, and wasteful.
Its members believe the Mirage abandoned confirmed survivors in order to chase answers that may never exist. They can point to years of Mirage expeditions that produced relics, fragments, and stories, but no dependable salvation.
Even so, the Order needs what the Mirage carries: forbidden-site access, field records, and the courage to enter regions the Order refuses to study.
That dependence is the heart of the reunification path in The Oasis.

project-zaman/lore/concepts/concepts-ind.title: Concepts Index
project-zaman/lore/concepts/concepts-ind.content:
Concepts Index
Tags: project-zaman lore concept index active


                  
                  Purpose of this folder 
                  
                

One note per metaphysical or philosophical concept in Project ZAMAN. Concepts are the rules of the world: what a thing is and why it behaves as it does.
Keep events in Lore/Events and systems the player interacts with in Lore/Mechanics. A concept explains; a mechanic operates.



Established Concepts
These are already defined elsewhere in the vault. Each deserves its own note; the source is listed so nothing has to be reconstructed from memory.


















































ConceptShort definitionDefined inImmaculate ThoughtCognition operating at extreme speed, clarity, and internal consistency. Not time manipulation; the cult preserves that false framing deliberately.Gibborim, MC, Project ZamanSoul FissionThe division of one soul into incomplete fragments under intolerable contradiction.MC, Axios, Oscillation of Eras[[Oscillation of ErasThe Oscillation of Eras]]The permanent desynchronization of reality caused when both soul-forms destabilized at once. Also called the Catastrophe.[[Irreversibility PrincipleThe Irreversibility Principle]]Nothing is restored. Only adaptation is possible. Held as doctrine by Gibborim, who plan around the permanence.Hope as IntegrationHope is carrying the whole self forward, not restoration and not escape.Themes, The Hope EntityThe Soul-FormsTwo competing responses within one consciousness: the compassionate form and the [[Shadow Formshadow form]]. Not two complete souls.[[DesertThe Desert]]Subject-001’s inner psychological landscape, inherited from the original MC. Its terrain shifts with his coherence.[[Fabrication DemiseThe Fabrication Demise]]The widespread loss of population following the Catastrophe. The deaths remain largely unconfirmed.

Open Questions

What does “Zaman” name? The Project Zaman naming framework reserves Arabic for core metaphysical truths and protagonist-facing ideas, but no Arabic term is currently defined anywhere in the vault. Is Zaman a concept characters can speak of in-world, or only the project’s title?
Is there an Arabic vocabulary at all yet? The framework promises one. At present Hebrew (Gibborim) and Greek (Anthropos, Axios) are the only languages with actual terms behind them. This is the largest unfilled gap in the naming system.
What exactly is the Fabrication Demise? The Oasis establishes its consequences — an unaccounted-for population, and a moral fault line between the two successor factions — but not its nature. Were people destroyed, displaced, desynchronized, or something else? The Order’s denial only works dramatically if the answer is genuinely uncertain in-world.
Is temporal desynchronization one condition or several? Colliding eras, distorted regions, and blind spots in perception are all described. Are these the same phenomenon at different scales?
What are time fragments, materially? They exist as prototype samples and as an extractable resource. Whether they are objects, energy, or something else is not stated.

Immaculate Thought is an extreme state of cognition in which thought approaches absolute speed, clarity, and internal consistency.
It is not true time manipulation.
The cult preserves the language of temporal control because that false interpretation gives Gibborim power over how subjects understand themselves and gives Axios a measurable framework for experimentation.

In the original MC, Immaculate Thought expresses itself through the three miracles:

Perceptual Time Quantification.
Epistemological Object Contact.
Silent Connection.

project-zaman/lore/concepts/irreversibil.content:
Irreversibility Principle
Tags: project-zaman lore concept irreversibility adaptation theme established
”Nothing is restored. What remains must learn how to continue.”
Category: Metaphysical and thematic law
Status: Established
Related: Themes, Open Gaps, Oscillation of Eras, The Hope Entity, The Oasis

Definition
The Irreversibility Principle states that the damage caused by the Oscillation of Eras cannot be undone.
Time cannot be restored. Alyna cannot return. The original MC cannot become whole again. The pre-Oscillation world is not waiting to be recovered.

Narrative Function
This principle protects the core theme of Project ZAMAN:

Hope is integration, not restoration.

The story is not about reversing trauma. It is about continuing after irreversible damage without allowing that damage to become the whole identity.

Faction Relevance
Gibborim treats the principle as doctrine and plans around permanence.
The Oasis and its child factions live inside the consequences of the principle, even when they disagree over whether survival depends on protection, knowledge, or reunification.

project-zaman/lore/concepts/soul-fission.content:

”One person divided into consequences.”
Category: Metaphysical rupture
Status: Established
Related: MC, Subject-001, Subject-002, The Hope Entity, Oscillation of Eras

Definition
Soul Fission is the division of one unified existence into incomplete fragments under intolerable contradiction.
In Project ZAMAN, it occurs when the original MC’s opposing soul-forms destabilize during the Oscillation of Eras.

Result
Soul Fission creates:

Subject-001, who carries the clearest emotional and moral continuity.
Subject-002, who carries the original body, the straitjacket, and physical trauma.
The Hope Entity, which remains as the preserved childhood self inside the Desert.

The division is not clean. Each fragment carries traces that complicate any simple claim to being the original MC.

What It Is Not
Soul Fission is not cloning, resurrection, reincarnation, or restoration.
It is a catastrophic distribution of body, soul, memory, trauma, and identity after the original unity can no longer survive.

Oscillation of Eras
Tags: project-zaman lore event catastrophe time irreversibility established
”The world did not rewind. It came apart and stayed that way.”
When: Final catastrophe before the post-Oscillation era
Where: The cult facility
Participants: MC, Noam, Axios, Gibborim

What Happens
The Oscillation of Eras occurs when the original MC’s opposing soul-forms destabilize at the same time under maximum experimental pressure.
Noam orders the procedure to continue despite warnings. The contradiction inside the MC’s soul becomes metaphysically real, reality desynchronizes, and different historical eras begin colliding in the same world.

Cause
The immediate trigger is the reveal of the Eleventh Chamber, where Alyna’s preserved body is used against the MC.
The deeper cause is the cult’s long misuse of Immaculate Thought, its extraction systems, and Noam’s refusal to accept failure.

Consequence

The original MC fractures into Subject-001 and Subject-002.
The facility becomes a decayed temporal ruin.
On-site cult personnel die.
Reality remains permanently desynchronized.
The Irreversibility Principle becomes unavoidable.
The survivor era begins, eventually leading to The Oasis.


What It Is Not
The Oscillation is not a reset, a cycle, or a repairable timeline error.
It is the permanent state the rest of the story must inhabit.

Function
